newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Dollar deluge to Brazil seen slowing.
newsitem.headline: Dollar deluge to Brazil seen slowing.

text.p: Dollar flows to Brazil, once a chief worry among policy-makers who feared their inflationary impact, should slow dramatically this month and remain modest through the end of the year, debt and currency traders said.

"There could always be an unexpected inflow due to direct foreign investment, but now we're working with a (net dollar flow) figure closer to equilibrium each month," said Deniz Pignatari, director of currency trading at ING Bank in Brazil.
Falling domestic interest rates, declining Eurobond issuance by banks and a busy Eurobond retirement calendar were seen as the main factors limiting net dollar surpluses through the rest of the year.

So far in September, dollar flows have posted an $87 million deficit, although most traders think the month will end in surplus. Large outflows in the first two weeks have gone toward retiring Eurobonds and making coupon payments.

Pignatari and others say the September-December period should post modest monthly dollar surpluses. But they will fall short of August's $1.5 billion surplus and not come anywhere near the $2.1 billion average monthly surplus from January through August, traders said.
"Interest rates aren't so high anymore so it's making less sense to go abroad and bring money back," said one currency dealer.

Eurobond traders said issuance by Brazilian banks has declined significantly due to falling interest rates and Central Bank restrictions on foreign debt issues implemented earlier this year. At the same time, a large number of Eurobonds will be retired over the next three months, leading to substantial dollar outlfows, they added.

The latest trend should please Central Bank officials, who have had to issue billions of dollars worth of domestic debt this year to "sterilize" dollar flows, or prevent them from expanding the money supply.

Economists estimate it costs the government $100 million in debt financing charges for every $1.0 billion in dollar inflows. The steady flows, which have swelled Brazil's foreign reserves to about $60 billion from $50 billion in January, pressure the country's mounting stock of internal debt, now at about 210 billion reais.

The current situation is in sharp contrast to the beginning of the year, when the Central Bank was facing monthly dollar surpluses of $2 billion to $3 billion. The money was drawn by arbitrage opportunities offered by wide spreads between domestic and international interest rates, which have since narrowed.
